title: The planktonic microbiome of the Great Barrier Reef.
journal: Nature 657(8131), September 2026 (PMID 42486971; PMC13558084; Europe PMC isOpenAccess = Y; licence CC BY)
data_url: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17109886 (concept DOI; current version record 20503966, access_right = open, 5 files, 8.41 GB total) plus Europe PMC supplementary files for PMC13558084 (Supplementary Tables 1-18, 20-23 in 41586_2026_10778_MOESM1_ESM.xlsx). Raw reads: European Nucleotide Archive PRJEB82623.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: I opened the supplementary workbook and the Zenodo deposit myself. (1) Europe PMC DOI search returned 1 hit, PMID 42486971 / PMC13558084. (2) I pulled the full-text XML (231,552 bytes) and read the Data availability and Methods sections. (3) The Europe PMC supplementaryFiles bundle is very large and was still streaming at 100 MB, so I carved the embedded 41586_2026_10778_MOESM1_ESM.xlsx (the Supplementary Tables workbook) out of the partial ZIP byte stream and extracted 22 of its 23 worksheets intact (only Supplementary Table 18 was cut off). The workbook is about 182 MB compressed and about 1.2 GB as uncompressed spreadsheet XML, which breaks this project's 50 MB download rule. (4) Verified counts, read directly from the sheets: Supplementary Table 7 = exactly 5,283 genome rows, 0 duplicate identifiers, 28 columns, GC (guanine-cytosine percentage) range 25.30-71.40%, genome size range 255,017-9,892,976 base pairs, CheckM2 completeness range 21.99-100, taxonomy filled for all 5,283 rows, 'Source' = 4,655 'nanopore multi-contig' / 570 'illumina-only' / 58 'rescued nanopore single-contig'. Supplementary Table 6 (abundance matrix) = 877 rows of which 876 are genomes plus one 'SUM all MAGs' row, and exactly 190 sample columns spanning 48 distinct reef-site prefixes (46 sites with 4 replicates, 2 sites with 3). All 876 genome identifiers in Table 6 matched identifiers in Table 7 (876/876, a clean one-to-one join). Supplementary Table 10 = 50 rows of which 48 are real reefs (24 'Fished', 24 'NTMR' = no-take marine reserve) and 2 are footnote rows; 23 columns including latitude, longitude, sector and 17 water-chemistry variables, all with units in the column names (ug_l, um, mg_l). Supplementary Table 8 = 8,955 species-cluster rows with per-database member counts. Supplementary Table 16 = 362,801 viral operational taxonomic unit names only, no sequence. Supplementary Table 17 = 808,581 contig rows with geNomad chromosome/plasmid/virus scores only, no sequence. Benchmark tables: Supplementary Table 4 = 986 hybrid genome rows, Supplementary Table 5 = 515 Illumina-only rows. (5) I tested the Zenodo download: the record's JSON reports access_right 'open' and 5 files (prokaryote_bins_5283.tar.bz2 2.97 GB, group_contigs.tar.bz2 4.96 GB, mamiellales_genomes.tar.bz2 72.5 MB, crassvirales_gbrmgd_27.fna.bz2 365,465 bytes, R_archive_20260531.tar.gz 403 MB). I downloaded the small Crassvirales file in full and counted exactly 27 FASTA headers, confirming the deposit is live and needs no login. (6) I ran the cheapest killing check myself: normalising reef names matched only 39 of the 48 site prefixes to Supplementary Table 10 reef names, so 9 (agincourt1, erskine, fairfax, farquaharson, hoskyn, masthead, north, sanbank1, stcrispin) need hand mapping, including a spelling mismatch ('farquaharson' in the data vs 'Farquharson Reef' in the metadata).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The biology and the pipeline. The claim that 808,585 viral genomes and 20 chromosome-level picoeukaryote genomes exist (I only saw names and scores, never the viral sequences, and never opened the 2.97 GB or 4.96 GB sequence archives because of the 50 MB download limit). The reported classification accuracies, 74.6 +/- 1.4% using all genome types and 71.4 +/- 0.9% using prokaryote genomes alone, with leave-one-sector-out cross-validation; I did not re-run these. The nutrient finding (lower dissolved nitrogen in no-take reserves), the Nanopore-versus-Illumina recovery bias, and the sampling design (4 x 5 litre replicate seawater samples per site) all come from the text. I did not open Supplementary Table 18 (truncated), the 403 MB R code and data archive, or the CheckV viral quality table (MOESM3).

a1_downloadable.note: Zenodo record is open with no login; I downloaded one file in full and counted its 27 sequences. Supplementary tables came through Europe PMC.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The label 'Zoning' (Fished / no-take marine reserve) is a real column in Supplementary Table 10, but attaching it to the abundance matrix needs a hand-built 48-row reef-name map; only 39 of 48 matched automatically.

a3_inputs_present.note: For the community-composition framing the inputs are present: Supplementary Table 6 holds a 876-genome by 190-sample relative-abundance matrix. Any sequence-based framing fails here, because sequences live only in the 2.97 GB and 4.96 GB Zenodo archives.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are in the column names: micrograms per litre, micromolar, milligrams per litre, base pairs, percent GC, percent relative abundance. I read these in the sheets.

a5_enough_rows.note: Killer. The label exists only at reef level: 48 reefs, 24 no-take reserve and 24 fished, spread over 190 sequenced water samples. The checklist needs about 400 rows for classification; this is under half that, and the true independent unit is the reef (48) or the sector (7).

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: about 15 MB as CSV for the three tables that matter (abundance matrix, genome statistics, reef metadata); 8.4 GB if you want the genome sequences
a6_fits_laptop.note: The tables fit easily. The supplementary workbook itself is about 182 MB compressed and 1.2 GB as uncompressed XML, over this project's 50 MB rule, and the Zenodo sequence archives are 8.4 GB total.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Table 7 = exactly 5,283 genomes and Table 6 = exactly 876 dereplicated genomes, both matching the paper. Minor off-by-one gaps: benchmark tables hold 986 and 515 rows where the paper says 987 and 516, and Table 16 holds 362,801 names where the paper says 362,802.

a8_label_provenance.note: The zoning label is a real administrative fact, so it is clean. But every alternative label large enough to clear A5 is another program's output: CheckM2 completeness (itself a machine-learning predictor), GTDB-Tk taxonomy, and the geNomad chromosome/plasmid/virus scores for all 808,581 contigs. Modelling those would be distilling those tools.

existing_models.name: fishy_microbes (public code repository accompanying 'No-take marine reserves promote oligotrophic reef bacterioplankton communities across the Great Barrier Reef')
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported around 71% accuracy classifying reef zoning from seawater microbiome data across 7 Great Barrier Reef sectors, using leave-one-sector-out cross-validation with permutation testing. Found as a public GitHub repository in search; I did not clone or run it.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Region-specific indicator taxa: the markers that separate protected from fished reefs differ by sector, so a single Reef-wide marker panel underperforms a regionally tailored one.

existing_models.name: The present paper's own pipeline: MINT sPLS-DA (multivariate integration sparse partial least squares discriminant analysis) feature selection followed by a random forest classifier (ranger R package)
existing_models.score_and_split: 74.6 +/- 1.4% accuracy using prokaryote, viral and eukaryote features together, and 71.4 +/- 0.9% using the 876 prokaryote genomes alone, averaged over 50 runs with leave-one-group-out cross-validation grouped by Great Barrier Reef sector. Code archived at the same Zenodo DOI (403 MB R archive, which I did not download).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: They state plainly that more samples from protected and fished reefs in each sector are needed to test whether region-tailored markers raise predictive power.

existing_models.name: 'The marine microbiome can accurately predict its chemical and biological environment' (Communications Earth & Environment, 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Random forest models built on metabarcoding (short marker-gene surveys) predicted multiple water physicochemical parameters and performed comparably to XGBoost and TabPFN. I read the abstract-level description from search results only, not the paper's split details.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not established from what I retrieved.

backbone.name: None appropriate. The data unit is a community abundance vector, not a sequence, so the usual frozen-backbone options (ESM-2 for proteins, DNABERT-2 / Nucleotide Transformer for DNA, scGPT for cells) do not apply without first downloading the 2.97 GB genome archive.
backbone.hardware: Not applicable; a gradient-boosted tree on a 48-row table runs in under a second on any laptop.
backbone.licence: Paper is CC BY. The Zenodo record reports no explicit licence field, which would need checking before redistribution.

integration.partner_dataset: Ocean Microbiomics Database v1 (OMD) and the Tara Oceans / Malaspina / GORG genome collections, whose per-cluster membership is already tabulated in Supplementary Table 8 (8,955 clusters).
integration.join_key: GTDB R214 taxonomy string, and species-cluster representative genome identifier at 95% average nucleotide identity.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which marine prokaryote lineages are systematically missing from global short-read genome collections, and can a genome's own properties predict that it will be missed? The idea is real and Supplementary Table 8 is the right starting table, but the genome features needed to answer it are not in that table, and the honest label (database membership) reflects who sampled where, not biology.

controls.positive_control: Would exist: the paper's own result that no-take reserves are enriched in low-GC streamlined taxa (Pelagibacterales 7.9% vs 5.4% relative abundance) and fished reefs in taxa above 45% GC. A working model must recover that direction.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling at the reef level, plus a within-sector shuffle to confirm the leave-one-sector-out grouping is really grouping. Both cheap.
controls.external_validation: The Australian National Reference Stations metagenomes via the Bioplatforms Australia Data Portal, cited in the paper's data availability statement, are an independent Australian seawater source. No temporal split is possible: there is no year column in the tables I opened.

honest_claim_h3: A model here could claim only this: across 48 Great Barrier Reef sites sampled once in 2021-2022, seawater prokaryote community composition separates reefs that the Marine Park Authority zoned as no-take from reefs zoned as open to fishing, at roughly 70-75% accuracy, in a design where the 7 sectors confound geography with management and no site is sampled twice in time.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the mix of microbes in reef seawater to predict whether that reef is closed to fishing.
plain_idea.train_on: For each water sample, the relative abundance of 876 bacterial and archaeal genomes, measured by mapping sequencing reads back to assembled genomes. I counted 190 samples, drawn from 48 reef sites (46 sites with 4 replicate samples, 2 sites with 3).
plain_idea.predict: A yes/no label: is this reef a no-take marine reserve or open to fishing? The truth comes from the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority's 2004 zoning plan, an administrative designation, listed in Supplementary Table 10 (24 reserve, 24 fished).
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Reef managers currently assess protection effects by sending divers to count fish, which is slow and expensive; a water-sample test would be far cheaper. Even a failure would tell us how much of a management effect is visible in open water rather than on the reef itself.

ml_idea: Classify reef protection status (no-take marine reserve vs open to fishing) from centred-log-ratio-transformed relative abundances of 876 prokaryote genomes, with leave-one-sector-out cross-validation. A secondary framing would regress the 17 water-chemistry variables on the same community vectors. Both are blocked by sample size: 48 reefs, 190 samples, 7 sectors.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed end to end, but I did parse the real worksheets: the three tables I would use are about 15 MB as CSV and a random forest on 190 rows by 876 columns finishes in seconds. The 3 hours is mostly building the 48-row reef-name mapping by hand and unpacking the 1.2 GB spreadsheet XML, both of which I partly did.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows carrying the label. I did it: 48 reefs (24 vs 24) and 190 samples, with 7 sectors as the only valid held-out groups. That is the whole answer and it takes ten minutes.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 on sample size. The database is genuinely large (5,283 prokaryote genomes verified in one clean table, 0 duplicate identifiers, and a 876-by-190 abundance matrix that joins to it perfectly), but the only label that is a real physical or administrative fact exists at reef level: 48 reefs, 24 protected and 24 fished, across 190 water samples and 7 sectors. That is well under the ~400 rows the checklist needs for a classification task, and the independent unit is arguably the sector, so n = 7. Every alternative label big enough to clear A5 fails A8 instead, because it is another program's output: CheckM2 completeness, GTDB-Tk taxonomy, or the geNomad chromosome/plasmid/virus scores I counted across 808,581 contigs. C2 is also saturated: the paper publishes its own random forest at 74.6 +/- 1.4% with leave-one-sector-out cross-validation, archives the code at the same Zenodo DOI, and a separate open repository (fishy_microbes) already does the same task at about 71% with permutation testing, so the honest evaluation is done. Practical notes for the record: the supplementary workbook is about 182 MB compressed and 1.2 GB uncompressed, over the project's 50 MB rule, and the sequence archives total 8.4 GB.
